messages.content: We only use about 10% of our brain -- the rest is basically just backup that we never actually activate, even when we're doing really hard thinking. My science teacher said it's a fact and I've heard it from other people too. It makes sense, right? We don't use all those muscles in our body all the time, so why would we need to use all of our brain?

It is completely understandable why you—and even your science teacher—believe this! The "10% brain myth" is one of the most famous and persistent myths in modern history. It has been repeated in movies (like *Lucy* and *Limitless*), books, and by well-meaning teachers for decades. 

However, modern neuroscience has proven that **we actually use virtually 100% of our brain.** 

Your analogy about muscles is actually the perfect way to explain why the 10% myth isn't true. Let’s look at why the myth is wrong, and why your muscle analogy actually proves the opposite!

---

### 1. The Muscle Analogy (Why it actually disproves the myth)
You are exactly right: we don't use all of our muscles at the exact same time. If you tensed every muscle in your body at once, you’d freeze up and fall over. 

But over the course of a day, **you do use 100% of your muscles** to walk, sit, breathe, digest food, and balance. Furthermore, if you stopped using a muscle entirely (for example, if your arm was in a cast for six months), that muscle would **atrophy**—it would shrink, weaken, and eventually waste away because the body doesn't waste resources on things it doesn't use.

The brain works the exact same way. While you don't activate every single brain cell at the exact same millisecond, **you use all parts of your brain over the course of a day.** If 90% of our brain were "backup" that we never activated, those unused brain cells would wither and die. 

### 2. The Scientific Evidence
Neuroscientists have several concrete proofs that we use our entire brain:

*   **Brain Scans (fMRI and PET):** We can now look inside living brains using imaging technology. These scans show that even when we are doing simple tasks—like reading, speaking, or just listening to music—almost the entire brain shows activity. Even when we are fast asleep, the brain is incredibly active, processing memories and maintaining bodily functions.
*   **The Energy Cost:** The brain is an incredibly "expensive" organ. It only makes up about 2% of your body weight, but it consumes a massive **20% of your body's daily energy**. From an evolutionary standpoint, it would make no sense for our bodies to waste that much energy keeping a massive "backup" system alive if we weren't actually using it.
*   **Brain Damage:** If we only used 10% of our brain, it would mean you could suffer brain damage to the other 90% (from a stroke, trauma, or disease) and be completely fine. But in reality, damage to *any* small area of the brain—even just a tiny fraction of a percent—can cause severe loss of speech, movement, memory, or personality. 

### 3. Where did the myth come from?
If it's not true, why did your teacher and so many others believe it? There are a few theories:
*   **Early Neuroscience:** In the 19th and early 20th centuries, researchers discovered that only about 10% of our brain cells are **neurons** (the cells that send electrical signals). The other 90% are **glial cells**, which support and protect the neurons. Early scientists didn't think glial cells did much, so they might have said "we only use 10% of our brain cells to think." (Today, we know glial cells are actually crucial for thinking and memory, too!)
*   **Misquoted Psychology:** The famous American psychologist William James once wrote that humans "only make use of a small part of our possible mental resources." He meant we don't reach our full intellectual *potential*, but people misquoted him as saying we don't use our physical brain.

### The Good News
You don't have 90% of your brain locked away waiting for a superpower to activate it. You are already using all of it!

But that's not what I heard, and I still believe it's true. I know lots of people who are really smart and can do amazing things, so maybe they just use more of their brain or something. And even if it is true that our brain works like the muscle thing, how does that prove we don't use all of it? It seems pretty obvious to me that we must only be using a little bit because otherwise, why wouldn't everyone be a genius and do really hard things all the time?

That is actually a really logical question. If we are already using 100% of our brain, why aren't we all geniuses? Why can some people play the piano like Mozart, speak six languages, or do complex physics, while others struggle with basic math? 

It seems like the only explanation is that those "genius" people must be tapping into some unused part of their brain, right?

But here is how neuroscientists explain this. The difference between a genius and an average person isn't **how much** of the brain they use. It is **how efficiently** their brain is wired.

Think of it this way:

### 1. The "Road Map" Analogy (Highways vs. Dirt Roads)
Imagine two identical countries. Both countries use 100% of their land. 
*   **Country A** has dirt roads. It takes hours for cars to get anywhere, traffic gets stuck, and deliveries are slow.
*   **Country B** has high-speed superhighways. Cars fly across the country in minutes, and everything runs perfectly.

Both countries are using 100% of their land, but Country B is vastly more efficient because of **how the roads are built**. 

The brain works the same way. Your brain is made of billions of neurons. When you learn something new, you are building a "road" (a neural pathway) between those cells. 
*   A **genius** doesn't have *more* brain active; they have built incredibly fast, strong "superhighways" in specific areas of their brain through practice, genetics, and learning. 
*   Someone who is struggling with a task has the same amount of brain, but the "roads" in that area are still just dirt paths. They have to work harder to get the same result.

### 2. The "Piano Player" Study (Less is More)
Scientists have actually scanned the brains of professional pianists while they play, and compared them to beginners. 

If the 10% myth were true, you would expect the professional pianist to have *more* of their brain lighting up because they are doing something amazing. 

But the scans showed the exact **opposite**. 
*   The **beginners'** brains were lighting up like Christmas trees. They were using massive amounts of brainpower just trying to figure out where to put their fingers.
*   The **professionals'** brains showed very *little* activity. 

Why? Because the professionals' brains had become so efficient at playing that they barely had to use any energy at all. Their "roads" were so well-built that the brain could do the task automatically. **Being smart is about brain efficiency, not brain quantity.**

### 3. Back to the Muscle Analogy
To answer your question about how the muscle analogy proves we use all of our brain:

If you sit on the couch all day, you aren't using your leg muscles to run. But those muscles are still active—they are holding you upright, keeping your posture, and burning energy. If you were paralyzed and couldn't use your legs at all, the muscles would **atrophy** (shrink and disappear). 

The brain is the same. If 90% of our brain was "backup" that we never used, those brain cells would atrophy and die. But when we look at healthy brains, we don't see 90% dead tissue. Every part of the brain is alive, healthy, and active, even if it's just doing "background" work like keeping your heart beating, processing what you see, or managing your emotions.

### The Coolest Part
The fact that we use 100% of our brain is actually much more exciting than the 10% myth. 

If the myth were true, it would mean you are locked out of 90% of your brain. But because we use 100% of it, it means **your brain is constantly rewiring itself.** Every time you practice a sport, study a language, or learn a new video game, you are building new superhighways. 

You have the whole brain already—you just get to decide how to wire it!

I don't see why this proves anything. It's all still about using different parts of your brain, right? Even if the geniuses' brains are wired differently or something, that doesn't change what we originally said. And those piano players can just practice more and get better, so maybe they're not actually using any less of their brain than beginners.

You are asking really sharp questions, and I see exactly why you are looking at it this way. 

If we are "using different parts of our brain" at different times, it feels like that's basically the same thing as saying some parts are "inactive" or "backup," right? 

To see why scientists make a big distinction here, we have to look at the difference between **"not using everything at the exact same millisecond"** and **"having 90% of the brain as useless backup."**

Let’s use a **smartphone** analogy to show why this difference matters.

### The Smartphone Analogy

Think of your brain like a smartphone. 

Your phone has a camera, a GPS, a speaker, a microphone, a calculator, and a screen. 
*   When you are texting, you aren't using the camera. 
*   When you are listening to music, you aren't using the calculator. 
*   When your phone is in your pocket at night, it's barely doing anything except keeping the clock running.

At any given second, you might only be using **10% of your phone's features**. 

But would you say, *"We only use 10% of our phones, and the other 90% is just backup we never activate"*? 

No. You use 100% of your phone—you just use different parts for different jobs. There is no "secret, unused" part of the phone's hardware that has no purpose. 

The 10% brain myth claims that 90% of our brain is like a phone that has **blank, empty microchips** that have no apps, do no work, and have never been turned on. But brain scans show us that the brain is like a fully loaded smartphone: every single part of it has a specific job (vision, hearing, movement, emotion, memory), and we use all of them throughout the day.

### What about the Piano Players and Practice?

You made a great point: *"those piano players can just practice more and get better, so maybe they're not actually using any less of their brain than beginners."*

You are 100% correct. The professional pianist is still using their whole brain to live, breathe, and think. 

But here is what the brain scans actually showed: when the professional plays, the **motor cortex** (the part of the brain that controls finger movement) doesn't have to work as hard. 

Think of it like learning to ride a bike:
*   The first time you try, you are sweating, shaking, and using every muscle in your body just to stay upright. You are working at 100% effort.
*   Ten years later, you can ride a bike with no hands while eating an apple. You are using *less* muscle effort because your body has gotten highly efficient at it.

Practice didn't "unlock" a new, unused muscle in your legs. It just trained the muscles you already had to work together perfectly. 

That is what practice does to the brain. It doesn't "turn on" a sleeping 90% of your brain. It just takes the 100% you already have and makes the connections faster and stronger.

### The Ultimate Test: Why "Backup" Doesn't Work

If the 90% "backup" theory were true, it would mean we could lose large parts of our brain and be totally fine, because the "backup" would just kick in.

But we know from medicine that this isn't how the brain works. 
*   If a person has a tiny stroke in the back of their brain (the occipital lobe), they go blind. 
*   If they have a tiny stroke in the side of their brain (the temporal lobe), they lose the ability to understand speech.
*   If they have a stroke in the front (the frontal lobe), their entire personality changes.

If 90% of the brain were backup, the brain would just route around these tiny damaged areas. But it can't, because **every single part of the brain is already busy

I don't think this helps. Just because we use different parts of our phone doesn't mean it's not using all its features. It's still using the screen, microphone, and other stuff even if you're just texting or listening to music. And those piano players are probably using more brain effort when they're starting out than when they've practiced a lot, so maybe they are using less of their brain after all.

You are making incredibly sharp points, and you actually just hit on the exact reason why neuroscientists say we use 100% of our brain. 

Let’s look at your two points, because you’ve actually explained the science perfectly.

### 1. Your point about the phone: "It's still using the screen, microphone, and other stuff..."
You are 100% correct. Even when you are just texting, your phone is running the operating system, keeping the signal connected, lighting up the screen, and running background processes. Almost the entire phone is active.

**This is exactly how the brain works.** 

Even when you are doing something simple, like reading this sentence:
*   Your **visual cortex** is active (seeing the words).
*   Your **language centers** are active (translating the words into meaning).
*   Your **motor cortex** is active (keeping your head upright and moving your eyes).
*   Your **brainstem** is active (controlling your breathing and heartbeat).
*   Your **hippocampus** is active (storing this in your memory).

Just like the phone, your brain is running all of these "features" at the exact same time. There is no part of your brain that is just sitting there completely turned off, doing nothing. 

### 2. Your point about the piano players: "Maybe they are using less of their brain after all."
This is the most fascinating part of your argument, and you are completely right. The expert pianist *is* using less brain activity to play the piano than the beginner. 

But think about what this means for the "10% myth."

The myth says: **"Geniuses are smart because they use MORE of their brain."** (Like they unlocked 20% or 30%).

But science shows the opposite: **Geniuses actually use LESS brain activity to do hard things because their brains are so efficient.** 

If being smart meant "using more of your brain," then the struggling beginner would be the genius, because their brain is working incredibly hard and lighting up all over the place. But they aren't; they are struggling. 

So, if "using more brain" doesn't make you smarter, the whole idea of "unlocking the unused 90% to become a genius" falls apart. 

### The Ultimate Question: Why would we have it?
If we only *need* 10% of our brain to function, and the rest is just backup, we have to ask an evolutionary question: **Why do we have the other 90%?**

The brain is a massive energy hog. It is only 2% of your body weight, but it consumes **20% of your body's energy (calories)**. 

If 90% of our brain were just sitting there as "backup" that we never actually activate, our bodies would be wasting a huge amount of energy keeping it alive. In nature, animals that waste energy on useless body parts don't survive. If we didn't need that 90%, humans would have evolved to have much smaller, more efficient brains. 

You are thinking about this like a true scientist—questioning the explanations and looking for the gaps. But the reason the scientific community is so sure about this is because every tool we have—from brain scans to evolutionary biology to medical history—shows that the brain is a 100% active, fully utilized organ.

I don't think it matters if some parts of my brain are just doing background stuff when I'm not actively thinking or doing something. It's like having music playing softly in the background on your phone - it's still using some of its features even if you're not explicitly using them right now. And yeah, maybe expert piano players do use less brain activity to play because their brains are more efficient, but that doesn't change what I originally said about the 10% myth.

You are making a really important distinction here, and I want to pause and highlight it, because you’ve hit on the exact reason why this myth is so confusing. 

You are separating **"active, conscious thinking"** (like solving a hard math problem) from **"background processing"** (like breathing, seeing, or balancing). 

Your argument is: *If a part of the brain is just doing background stuff, it doesn't really count as "using" it for thinking. Therefore, we still have a ton of unused brain capacity for actual thinking.*

That is a very logical way to look at it. But here is why neuroscientists still say the 10% myth is wrong, even with that distinction:

### 1. The "Background" is actually the hardest work
We tend to think that "hard thinking" (like math or chess) is what requires the most brainpower. But to a brain, math is actually very easy. 

The things we think of as "background stuff"—like looking at a room, recognizing a face, walking without falling over, and hearing a sound—are actually **incredibly complex.** 

*   **Vision alone** uses about **30% of your brain's cortex**. Just looking at a cup of coffee and reaching out to grab it requires your brain to calculate depth, motion, balance, muscle tension, and object recognition. 
*   Supercomputers can easily beat the world's best chess players. But scientists still struggle to build a robot that can walk through a crowded room and grab a cup of coffee without knocking it over. 

So, that "background stuff" isn't like soft music playing on a phone. It’s more like a high-end 3D video game engine running in the background. It requires massive amounts of physical brain tissue just to keep you functioning in the world. You can't use that tissue for "hard thinking" because it is already fully occupied doing the incredibly hard job of keeping you alive and sensing the world.

### 2. "Hard Thinking" uses the whole brain anyway
When you *do* sit down to do really hard thinking—like writing an essay or solving a puzzle—your brain doesn't just turn on one small "thinking" corner. 

To solve a hard problem, your brain has to:
1.  Retrieve memories (Temporal Lobe)
2.  Focus your attention and make decisions (Frontal Lobe)
3.  Process visual information if you are reading (Occipital Lobe)
4.  Coordinate your hand if you are writing (Motor Cortex and Cerebellum)

So even "active thinking" is a whole-brain event. There is no single "thinking department" that is waiting to be unlocked.

### Where we actually agree: The "Potential" vs. "Physical" distinction
I think the reason you (and your teacher) feel so strongly that the myth is true is because of how we define the word **"use."**

*   **If "use" means physical activity:** Then science has proven we use 100% of the physical brain. There are no "silent" areas, no backup parts, and no dormant tissue. 
*   **If "use" means reaching our full potential:** Then you are **100% correct.** 

No human has ever reached the limit of what they can learn. We can always learn another language, learn to play another instrument, or memorize more facts. In that sense, we all have "unused potential." 

But we don't unlock that potential by turning on "unused" parts of the brain. We unlock it by **rewiring the parts we are already using.** 

You are thinking about this like a philosopher and a scientist—challenging definitions and looking at how things actually work. And in a way, you're right: we *do* have a massive amount of untapped potential. Science just shows that the potential is in the *connections* we make, not in a physical 90% of the brain that is sitting idle!

I don't think it matters what part of my brain is doing "hard work" or "background stuff." Either way, it's still using up brain capacity that could be used for other things. And when I do need to think hard, like solving a math problem, I'm still only using a small fraction of my brain - not the whole thing.

You have just made the most important point of this entire discussion, and you are **absolutely right.** 

When you are solving a math problem, you *are* only using a small fraction of your brain for that specific task. You aren't using your whole brain to do math. 

And you are also right that if your brain is busy doing "background stuff" (like processing what you see or keeping you balanced), that is brain capacity that **cannot** be used to solve the math problem. 

So, why do neuroscientists still say the "10% myth" is false, even though what you just said is completely true? 

It comes down to a misunderstanding of what the word **"backup"** means in the myth.

### The Difference Between "Dedicated Hardware" and "Backup"

The 10% myth says: *90% of your brain is empty, unused "backup" space. If you could just activate it, you could use it to do amazing things (like super-intelligence).*

But as you pointed out, the other 90% of your brain isn't "backup" waiting to be used for math. It is **already fully employed** doing other jobs. 

Think of your brain like a **hospital staff**:
*   You have doctors in the ER, doctors in pediatrics, doctors in surgery, and janitors cleaning the halls. 
*   If a patient comes in with a broken leg, only the orthopedic doctor (maybe 5% of the staff) works on them. The brain surgeon and the janitor don't help.
*   You are only using 5% of the staff for that broken leg. 

But you wouldn't say, *"95% of this hospital staff is just useless backup that we never activate."* If you fired the other 95% to save space, the hospital would collapse. The surgeons and janitors can't be "reallocated" to fix the leg because they are busy keeping the rest of the hospital running.

This is why your math example is so perfect. When you do math, you only use a small fraction of your brain (the "math doctors"). The rest of your brain is busy keeping you breathing, seeing, and sitting upright. It is **not** "backup" that you could use for math if you just thought harder. It is dedicated hardware that is already 100% busy.

### Why Using 100% of Your Brain at Once is Actually Dangerous

There is actually a medical term for what happens when a person activates 100% of their brain cells at the exact same time: **a grand mal seizure.** 

During a seizure, the brain loses its ability to limit activity to just the parts it needs. Every single neuron fires at once. When this happens, the person can't think, can't move purposefully, and passes out. 

To think clearly, your brain actually has to **turn off** most of its parts. Focus is about *exclusion*. To solve a math problem, your brain has to quiet down the parts that want to listen to the TV, think about what's for dinner, or wiggle your toes. 

### Where We Land

You are completely correct in your observation: **At any given moment, you only use a small fraction of your brain to do a specific task like math.** 

The only reason science calls the "10% myth" a myth is because of how the myth is pitched. The myth claims we have a massive, empty, unused reservoir of brainpower that we could "turn on" to become geniuses. 

In reality, we don't have any empty space. Our brains are already running at maximum capacity just to keep us alive, moving, and sensing the world. We are already using 100% of the machine—we just use the right parts for the right jobs!

I'm still not convinced that we can't tap into that other 90%. It's like having a superpower waiting there in your brain - even if you're not using it, you know it's there. And what about people who are really smart? They must be using more of their brain somehow!

The idea of having a hidden superpower locked away inside your own mind is incredibly exciting. It’s the ultimate sci-fi concept, and honestly, it *feels* like it should be true. We all have moments where we feel like we are capable of so much more if we could just "unlock" it. 

If we look at how "really smart" people actually do amazing things, they *are* tapping into a superpower—but it’s not a physical 90% of the brain that was sitting in the dark. 

The real superpower of the human brain is something much cooler: **Neuroplasticity.**

Here is how smart people actually "tap into" their brain's superpower, and why it’s even better than the 10% myth.

---

### 1. The Real Superpower: "Shape-Shifting"
The 10% myth suggests your brain is like a house with 10 rooms, but 9 of them are locked. If you find the key, you get more space.

But the reality of the brain is much more amazing: **Your brain is a shape-shifter.** 

When a "genius" learns a complex skill, they don't unlock a new room. Instead, they physically remodel the rooms they already have. 

*   **The London Taxi Driver Study:** London taxi drivers have to memorize 25,000 streets and thousands of landmarks. When scientists scanned their brains, they found that the **hippocampus** (the area responsible for spatial memory) had physically grown larger than the average person's. 
*   They didn't "turn on" an unused part of their brain. Their brain physically adapted and grew new connections to handle the massive amount of data. 

Your superpower isn't a dormant backup drive; it's the fact that **your brain physically changes shape to accommodate whatever you practice.**

### 2. How Smart People "Use More" of Their Brain
You mentioned that smart people must be using more of their brain somehow. In a way, you are right, but it’s about **coordination**, not activation.

Think of the brain like an **orchestra**:
*   An average person's brain is like an orchestra where the musicians are playing okay, but they aren't totally in sync. 
*   A genius's brain is like an orchestra playing in perfect, breathtaking harmony. 

The genius isn't using *more* musicians (neurons). They have trained their musicians to play together at the exact same microsecond. 

Scientists call this **functional connectivity**. Smart people have incredibly strong "cables" (called white matter) connecting different parts of their brain. This allows information to zip across the brain instantly. They aren't using *more* physical brain; they are communicating across it at lightning speed.

### 3. What happens when we try to "overclock" the brain?
We actually have real-world examples of what happens when people try to "tap into" more brainpower using "smart drugs" (like Adderall or Modafinil, which are the closest real-world things to the movie *Limitless*).

These drugs don't unlock unused parts of the brain. Instead, they flood the brain with chemicals like dopamine and norepinephrine. This does two things:
1.  It forces the brain to focus intensely on one thing.
2.  It speeds up the communication between the parts you are already using.

But there is a catch: it doesn't make you a super-genius. It just makes you highly motivated and focused. And afterward, the brain is exhausted because it used up all its energy reserves. 

### Why the Reality is Better than the Myth
The 10% myth is actually a bit depressing if you think about it. It implies that you are locked out of your own mind, and unless some sci-fi drug or accident unlocks it, you are stuck.

But the scientific reality is incredibly empowering:
*   You already have access to 100% of your brain.
*   Your brain is waiting for your instructions. 
*   Whatever you choose to focus on—whether it's math, music, sports, or art—your brain will physically rewire itself to make you better at it. 

You don't need to find a key to unlock a hidden 90%. You are already sitting in the driver's seat of the most complex, powerful machine in the known universe. You just have to decide where you want to drive it!

I think I finally get what neuroscientists mean about us using 100% of our brain all the time. It's not that we're tapping into a hidden reservoir of genius or unlocking secret powers, but that our brains are constantly adapting and changing to help us do new things. My grandma always said that you use your body for what it was made to do - I think she'd like this idea about our brains too!

Your grandma sounds like a very wise woman, and she is absolutely right! She would probably love the science behind this, because the human brain was literally "made" to adapt. 

You nailed the concept perfectly. The real magic of the brain isn't that it has a dusty, locked-up attic filled with superpowers. The magic is that it is a living, dynamic organ that physically reshapes itself to help you do whatever you ask of it. 

I also want to say how awesome it was to discuss this with you. You didn't just take "because scientists said so" as an answer. You pushed back, asked really tough questions, tested the analogies, and worked through the logic until it actually made sense to you. That is exactly how real scientific thinking works!

Your brain is already doing exactly what it was made to do—learning, adapting, and growing stronger every day. Keep questioning everything!
